text: Selling live poultry (ការលក់បសុបក្សីរស់) can go through farm-gate buyers (delivered poultry, less transport/handling for the farmer, but less bargaining power), village collectors/traders (aggregate multiple farmers' birds -- solves the common smallholder problem of not having enough volume alone), local markets, restaurants, slaughterers, or direct household sales. The right channel depends on flock size, bird type/age/weight, buyer requirements, and transport distance -- compare net return (price minus transport, cages, market fees, commissions, mortality, and rejected birds), not the quoted price alone; a lower farm-gate price sometimes produces the better actual return. Live-bird markets bring poultry from different farms together and are recognized (including by WOAH) as important disease surveillance points for avian influenza -- NEVER transport sick birds or birds from a flock with unexplained mortality to market just to recover some value; if unexplained deaths or serious disease signs appear, stop movement and get veterinary guidance first. Cambodian smallholder chickens include substantial local genetic diversity (documented types include Jai, Sompuwv, Skuoy, and fighting types), but village birds are frequently crosses -- do not assign a specific named breed to a farmer's birds without confirmation; record 'local/native chicken' or similar instead. Eggs (ស៊ុត) are a separate product needing protection from heat, breakage, and contamination rather than the same handling as live birds; for a smallholder selling locally, rapid sale is usually more practical than investing in cold storage. During the wet season, muddy transport and wet cages are the main problems; during the dry season, heat stress during transport is the main risk -- avoid transporting during the hottest hours. Do not invent a current local price, buyer, or breed premium; help the farmer compare actual offers instead.
